screens.title: Testing Strategies for Pattern‑Rich Codebases
screens.narratorSegment: Testing design-pattern-rich code is about more than passing green bars. Patterns introduce abstractions and collaborators, and good tests assure that those abstractions behave as intended and remain safe to change. In this chapter you'll learn practical approaches for unit testing Strategy, Factory, and Decorator implementations using xUnit and common mocking libraries. You will see how to isolate the unit under test, how to verify delegation and creation logic, and when an integration test is more appropriate than a pure unit test. We will emphasize realistic examples: verifying that a PaymentContext delegates to an IPaymentStrategy, ensuring a VehicleFactory creates the expected concrete type, and asserting that a LoggingNotifierDecorator logs before and after it delegates. Along the way you'll learn common pitfalls — like over-mocking or testing the pattern instead of the implementation — and concrete remedies such as balancing mocks with lightweight integration tests and leveraging dependency injection. By the end, you should be able to choose the right level of isolation for each test, write clear verification assertions, and design classes so they are straightforward to test. Consider how you would verify a single responsibility within a pattern: that focus will guide every test you write.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Learning Objectives
Skill outcomes
  • Interaction verification: Learn to assert calls, arguments, and call counts with Moq to confirm delegation.
  • Factory assertions: Test returned concrete types, expected messages, and exception paths to avoid silent failures.
  • Mock vs stub choice: Use stubs for simple returns, mocks when behavior and argument verification matter.
  • Test scope judgment: Choose unit tests for speed and isolation; reserve integration tests for critical end-to-end paths.
Common pitfall
Avoid tests that check "the pattern works" — instead check that your PaymentContext delegates correctly and that your factory returns the expected type for given inputs.

screens.title: Testing the Strategy Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: The Strategy pattern separates an algorithm behind a common interface so different implementations can be swapped at runtime. For testing, that separation is useful: you test each concrete strategy in isolation to confirm its algorithmic behavior, and you test the context to ensure it delegates to the injected strategy. A practical example is a payment system: concrete strategies implement IPaymentStrategy and a PaymentContext invokes ProcessPayment. In a unit test for PaymentContext, we replace the concrete strategy with a mock and verify that ProcessPayment was called with the right amount. This avoids invoking real payment flows and keeps the test fast and deterministic. For each concrete strategy, write focused tests that exercise the algorithm it implements — for example, a credit card strategy may format fees differently than a PayPal strategy. A common misconception is to test that the Strategy pattern itself functions rather than asserting your code's delegation and result handling; tests should prove that PaymentContext uses the strategy contract properly and that strategies produce correct outputs. Example assertions include verifying call counts and parameters and ensuring alternate strategies are honored after SetStrategy is called. As a takeaway, treat strategies as units to test directly and treat the context as the orchestration point whose job is delegation and handling the returned result or side effects.

keyIdea.title: Test strategies and delegation
keyIdea.text: Write unit tests for each concrete strategy and use mocks to verify that the context delegates with correct arguments and call counts.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Testing the Strategy Pattern
Code example (context test)
using Xunit;
using Moq;

public class PaymentContextTests
{
  [Fact]
  public void ExecutePayment_ShouldCallCreditCardStrategy()
  {
    var mockCreditCardStrategy = new Mock<IPaymentStrategy>();
    var context = new PaymentContext(mockCreditCardStrategy.Object);
    decimal testAmount = 100.0m;

    context.ExecutePayment(testAmount);

    mockCreditCardStrategy.Verify(s => s.ProcessPayment(testAmount), Times.Once());
  }
}
Explanation
  • Mock the strategy to avoid side effects and verify that ProcessPayment is called.
  • Test each concrete strategy separately to validate algorithmic differences.
  • When switching strategies at runtime, assert the context delegates to the new strategy.
Example scenario
A PaymentContext should call the injected CreditCardPayment strategy with the correct amount and not call any previous strategy after SetStrategy is used.
Key Takeaway

Focus tests on delegation and algorithm correctness rather than proving the pattern itself.

screens.title: Testing the Factory Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: Factory patterns centralize object creation, so tests must verify both the factory's decision logic and the created objects' behavior. When testing a factory, create tests that exercise different input parameters and assert the returned concrete type and its observable behavior. For example, a VehicleFactory that returns Car or Motorcycle should be tested with CreateVehicle("Car") and CreateVehicle("Motorcycle"), asserting type and behavior like GetDescription. You should also test failure paths like unknown inputs to ensure the factory throws appropriate exceptions. A common misconception is to test only the produced type and not the object's behavior; always follow up type assertions with behavior checks on the returned object to ensure it meets expectations. If a factory depends on collaborators, mock those dependencies and verify they are used correctly during creation. When the factory logic is simple, the tests are straightforward: assert type and output. If creation is more complex, include tests that examine the factory's interactions with its dependencies. Balancing these tests prevents regression in object composition and ensures the system receives correctly configured instances during runtime. Testing the Factory Pattern means factories should be tested for the correct concrete type, expected behavior on the returned object, and proper exception handling.. In practical terms, assert created types, return behavior, and error cases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Testing the Factory Pattern
Factory code (reference)
public class VehicleFactory
{
  public IVehicle CreateVehicle(string type)
  {
    if (type == "Car") return new Car();
    if (type == "Motorcycle") return new Motorcycle();
    throw new ArgumentException("Unknown vehicle type.");
  }
}

// Test should assert type and behavior:
// Assert.IsType<Car>(vehicle);
// Assert.Equal("I am a Car.", vehicle.GetDescription());
Testing checklist
  • Assert the returned concrete type for each input option.
  • Verify observable behavior on the returned object, not only its type.
  • Test exception or error paths for unknown inputs.
  • Mock dependencies of the factory if creation logic uses collaborators.
Analogy
Think of a factory test like checking both the box label and the product inside. Type is the label; behavior is the product.
Key Takeaway

Cover valid creation paths, behavior of produced objects, and failure cases to keep factories reliable.

screens.title: Testing the Decorator Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: A Decorator wraps a component to add responsibilities while preserving the wrapped component's interface. Testing a decorator requires asserting two things: first, that the decorator performs its additional behavior; second, that it delegates to the wrapped component so original behavior remains. For instance, a LoggingNotifierDecorator logs messages before and after calling the wrapped INotifier. In tests, replace the wrapped notifier and logger with mocks. Verify that the logger's LogInfo is called before and after, and that the wrapped notifier's Send is called exactly once with the expected message. A common mistake is to use the real wrapped component and real logger, which hides whether delegation and logging sequence are correct and complicates assertions. Use mocking to verify ordering and counts when the sequence matters. Another practical point: prefer verifying observable side effects or interaction counts rather than internal state. For critical paths, complement interaction tests with a light integration test using a ConsoleLogger or a fake logger to ensure the combined behavior looks correct in a more realistic run. This balanced approach keeps tests fast and trustworthy while guarding important sequences.

keyIdea.text: Mock both the wrapped component and collaborators like loggers. Assert the decorator calls the wrapped component and performs its additions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Testing the Decorator Pattern
Decorator example (reference)
public class LoggingNotifierDecorator : INotifier
{
  private readonly INotifier _wrappedNotifier;
  private readonly ILogger _logger;

  public LoggingNotifierDecorator(INotifier wrappedNotifier, ILogger logger)
  {
    _wrappedNotifier = wrappedNotifier;
    _logger = logger;
  }

  public void Send(string message)
  {
    _logger.LogInfo($"Before sending: {message}");
    _wrappedNotifier.Send(message);
    _logger.LogInfo($"After sending: {message}");
  }
}
Test structure
  • Arrange: Create mocks for INotifier and ILogger, then construct the decorator with those mocks.
  • Act: Call Send on the decorator with a test message.
  • Assert: Verify ILogger.LogInfo called twice and INotifier.Send called once with the message.
Common mistake
Using real loggers or real notifiers in unit tests converts them into integration tests and obscures interaction details.
Key Takeaway

Mock collaborators and assert both added behavior and delegation to the wrapped component to keep tests precise.

screens.title: Mocking and Stubbing Techniques
screens.narratorSegment: Mocking and stubbing are core techniques to isolate the unit under test. A stub provides canned responses and is useful when a collaborator returns predictable data you depend on. A mock, by contrast, is used when you want to verify how a dependency was used — the methods called, the arguments passed, and how often those calls occurred. In. NET, libraries like Moq make this straightforward: create Mock<T> objects, set up return values for stubs, and call Verify to assert interactions. Start each test by asking: do I care about the collaborator's behavior or only the interaction? If you only need a value, a stub suffices. If you need to assert a call sequence or argument values, use a mock with Verify. Avoid the anti-pattern of mocking everything; over-mocking can make tests brittle because internal changes in collaborators will break tests that shouldn't depend on those details. Instead, mock boundaries where your unit integrates with side effects, and keep simple data providers as lightweight fakes or stubs. When external services or databases are involved, use integration tests or well-controlled test doubles that mimic essential behavior without adding fragility. This decision process will keep tests fast, meaningful, and maintainable.

keyIdea.title: Choose the right double
keyIdea.text: Use stubs for predictable returns and mocks when you must verify interactions; avoid over-mocking to reduce brittle tests.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Mocking and Stubbing Techniques
Decision process (steps)
1
Do you need to verify calls?
If yes, use a mock and Verify. If no, a stub or fake is faster and simpler.
2
Is the dependency external or slow?
Replace it with a test double to keep unit tests deterministic and fast.
3
Avoid over-mocking
Mock only where behavior must be observed. Favor simple fakes for predictable data.
Moq tips
  • Use Setup to return values for stubs: mock.Setup(m => m.GetValue()).Returns(value);
  • Use Verify to assert interactions: mock.Verify(m => m.Send(It.IsAny<string>()), Times.Once());
  • Prefer It.Is<T> to assert argument shapes rather than exact instances when appropriate.
Example
Use a stub for a repository that returns static test data, and use a mock for a payment gateway where you must verify the call and amount passed.
Key Takeaway

Pick the simplest double that satisfies the assertion you care about. Keep tests fast and focused.

screens.title: Unit Tests vs Integration Tests
screens.narratorSegment: Unit tests and integration tests serve different goals and both matter in pattern-rich codebases. Unit tests isolate a small unit — typically a class — and verify its behavior in controlled conditions. They are fast, deterministic, and ideal for verifying delegation, algorithmic logic, and interaction with mocked collaborators. Integration tests, by contrast, verify how multiple components work together, possibly including database contexts, serialization, or external services (faked or real). For patterns like Factory, Strategy, and Decorator, unit tests confirm the internals and interactions, while a small set of integration tests can validate that constructed objects function correctly in realistic flows. A common error is relying only on integration tests; they can be slower and make it harder to find the exact failure point. Another mistake is using unit tests for scenarios that require end-to-end behavior, for example when database or configuration interactions are part of the correctness criteria. The recommended workflow is a large suite of focused unit tests for fast feedback, plus a smaller number of integration tests for confidence in critical paths. This mix keeps your feedback cycle short while ensuring the system behaves correctly when components are composed.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Unit Tests vs Integration Tests
Unit test characteristics
  • Isolated from external systems using mocks or stubs.
  • Fast to run and easy to diagnose when failures occur.
  • Ideal for verifying delegation, algorithms, and small behaviors.
Integration test characteristics
  • Verify multiple components together, including persistence and configuration.
  • Slower, but necessary for critical end-to-end validation.
  • Use for critical flows like payment processing with faked external services or an in-memory database.
Guideline
Favor many unit tests for quick feedback and a few targeted integration tests for confidence where composition or environment affects correctness.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls When Testing Pattern‑Rich Code
screens.narratorSegment: Pattern-rich code introduces abstraction layers and collaborators that can encourage test anti-patterns. One widespread pitfall is over-mocking: mocking every dependency, including simple data providers, which makes tests brittle because they depend on internal implementation details. Another mistake is testing the pattern rather than the implementation — for example, writing tests that assert "this is a Strategy" instead of verifying that PaymentContext calls ProcessPayment with the correct amount. Also, developers sometimes blur the line between unit and integration tests by allowing real services or databases into unit tests; that reduces speed and makes failures harder to diagnose. To avoid these problems, mock only those collaborators that produce side effects or whose behavior you must verify. Use stubs or simple fakes for data providers, and keep integration tests separate and limited in number. Finally, keep your assertions focused on observable behavior and public contracts. Tests that assert interactions, return values, and exception behavior provide clear documentation and safe refactor points without coupling to internal implementation details. Common Pitfalls When Testing Pattern‑Rich Code means mock only what you must verify, prefer behavior-focused assertions, and separate integration tests from unit tests.. In practical terms, over-mocking, testing the pattern, and blurred test scopes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Pitfall: Over-mocking
Mocking internal collaborators can make tests tightly coupled to implementation. Mock only boundaries that produce side effects or whose behavior you must assert.
Pitfall: Testing the pattern
Tests that assert "pattern presence" are less useful than tests that assert the observable behavior your application relies on.
Pitfall: Mis-scoped tests
Mixing external systems into unit tests makes them slow and fragile. Reserve integration tests for the flows that require them.
Key Takeaway

Be intentional about what you mock and why. Keep tests focused on behavior and public contracts to remain maintainable.

screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through writing a unit test for LoggingNotifierDecorator using xUnit and Moq. The goal is to assert that the logger's LogInfo is called twice — before and after sending — and that the wrapped notifier's Send is called once with the correct message. In your test project, create mocks for INotifier and ILogger, construct the decorator with those mocks, call Send with a test message, and then call Verify on both mocks. This isolates the behavior and makes the assertions precise. A concrete test verifies both ordering and counts: the test verifies two logger calls and one wrapped notifier call. Remember to keep the message content explicit in Verify when that's important to the behavior you want to enforce. If ordering matters, Moq allows sequences via setups or callbacks; however, many teams prefer verifying counts and presence rather than rigid ordering to reduce brittleness. After writing the test, run it and inspect the result. If it fails, focus on the specific assertion to guide a minimal fix. keyIdea.title: Practical test for a decorator
keyIdea.text: Mock the wrapped component and logger, call Send on the decorator, and Verify logger calls and wrapped notifier calls.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › LoggingNotifierDecorator Test
Test class template
using Xunit;
using Moq;

public class LoggingNotifierDecoratorTests
{
  [Fact]
  public void Send_ShouldLogBeforeAndAfterAndCallWrappedNotifier()
  {
    // Arrange
    var mockWrappedNotifier = new Mock<INotifier>();
    var mockLogger = new Mock<ILogger>();
    var decorator = new LoggingNotifierDecorator(mockWrappedNotifier.Object, mockLogger.Object);
    string testMessage = "Test Message";

    // Act
    decorator.Send(testMessage);

    // Assert
    mockLogger.Verify(l => l.LogInfo(It.Is<string>(s => s.Contains("Before sending: "))), Times.Once());
    mockWrappedNotifier.Verify(n => n.Send(testMessage), Times.Once());
    mockLogger.Verify(l => l.LogInfo(It.Is<string>(s => s.Contains("After sending: "))), Times.Once());
  }
}
Explanation
The test arranges mocks, constructs the decorator, acts by calling Send, then asserts three interactions: logger before, wrapped notifier send, and logger after. Using It.Is<string> lets you check message content without matching the exact interpolated string.
Pro tip
Prefer verifying presence and counts over strict ordering unless the sequence is critical to correctness.
Key Takeaway

This test pattern is reusable for other decorators. Mock external collaborators and assert added behavior plus delegation.

screens.title: Dependency Injection and Testability
screens.narratorSegment: Dependency Injection is a fundamental enabler of testability in pattern-based designs. When classes receive collaborators through constructors or properties rather than instantiating them directly, tests can easily supply mocks or stubs. For example, PaymentContext accepts an IPaymentStrategy in its constructor, which allows tests to pass a Mock<IPaymentStrategy> and verify interactions. Without DI, you would need to change production code to make it testable, which is undesirable. Use DI consistently for services, loggers, repositories, and factories so tests can swap implementations as needed. A typical testable design keeps object creation at composition roots and passes interfaces across layers. That keeps business logic free from infrastructure choices and makes unit tests straightforward. Remember a misconception: DI is not a silver bullet for poorly designed classes. Testability improves when classes have clear responsibilities and small constructor surfaces. Use DI to inject collaborators and write focused tests that exercise behavior and interactions. When writing tests, mimic the dependency graph minimally — mock only the collaborators that the unit interacts with directly and prefer small fakes for simple needs. This approach produces maintainable tests and code that scales as patterns and responsibilities evolve.

keyIdea.title: DI makes testing practical
keyIdea.text: Inject dependencies to swap real components for mocks or stubs in tests, keeping production code unchanged and tests isolated.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Dependency Injection & Testability
DI example
public class PaymentContext
{
  private IPaymentStrategy _paymentStrategy;

  public PaymentContext(IPaymentStrategy strategy)
  {
    _paymentStrategy = strategy;
  }

  public void SetStrategy(IPaymentStrategy strategy)
  {
    _paymentStrategy = strategy;
  }

  public void ExecutePayment(decimal amount)
  {
    _paymentStrategy.ProcessPayment(amount);
  }
}
Why DI helps tests
  • Replace real dependencies with mocks in unit tests without touching production code.
  • Keep construction at the application composition root and pass interfaces across layers.
  • Reduce test setup complexity and make intent explicit in each test.
Practical note
Favor small constructor surfaces: inject only the collaborators a class truly needs for single responsibility and easier test setup.
Key Takeaway

Design for testability by using DI and small, focused responsibilities. Tests become simpler and more resilient.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the most important ideas to carry forward. First, unit tests should isolate behavior: mock or stub collaborators so you can verify delegation, call counts, and argument values. Second, test factories by asserting produced types and observable behavior, and check failure paths for unknown inputs. Third, decorators require two kinds of checks: that they add their responsibilities and that they still delegate to the wrapped component. Use dependency injection throughout: it makes swapping mocks and stubs easy and keeps production code unchanged. Finally, avoid over-mocking and blurred test scopes; favor many focused unit tests for fast feedback, complemented by a few integration tests for critical end-to-end validation. These practices keep pattern-based systems reliable and refactor-friendly. As you write tests, always ask: what behavior am I protecting and what should break if I change the implementation? That question guides effective, maintainable tests.

fullNarratorScript:
Testing design-pattern-rich code is about more than passing green bars. Patterns introduce abstractions and collaborators, and good tests assure that those abstractions behave as intended and remain safe to change. In this chapter you'll learn practical approaches for unit testing Strategy, Factory, and Decorator implementations using xUnit and common mocking libraries. You will see how to isolate the unit under test, how to verify delegation and creation logic, and when an integration test is more appropriate than a pure unit test. We will emphasize realistic examples: verifying that a PaymentContext delegates to an IPaymentStrategy, ensuring a VehicleFactory creates the expected concrete type, and asserting that a LoggingNotifierDecorator logs before and after it delegates. Along the way you'll learn common pitfalls — like over-mocking or testing the pattern instead of the implementation — and concrete remedies such as balancing mocks with lightweight integration tests and leveraging dependency injection. By the end, you should be able to choose the right level of isolation for each test, write clear verification assertions, and design classes so they are straightforward to test. Consider how you would verify a single responsibility within a pattern: that focus will guide every test you write.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose appropriate testing approaches for classes that implement common design patterns. You will practice writing unit tests for Strategy, Factory, and Decorator examples, including how to create mocks and stubs with Moq. You will also recognize when a test should be an integration test instead of an isolated unit test and how to avoid common mistakes like testing the pattern rather than the implementation or over-mocking dependencies. Each objective pairs a practical skill — writing a verification for a delegated call, asserting factory outputs, or ensuring decorator behavior — with why it matters: maintainable, fast, and trustworthy tests that guide safe refactors. These skills will help you keep pattern-based code reliable while you extend or refactor it in real projects. Expect short exercises that reinforce each objective and a hands-on test you will walk through using xUnit and Moq.

This second objectives slide emphasizes concrete verification skills and common testing decisions. First, you will learn to write assertions that verify interactions: confirming that ProcessPayment was called with the expected amount or that a decorator invoked its wrapped component. This matters because interaction verification ensures your code delegates correctly without running side-effecting logic. Second, you will learn to test object creation paths in factories — asserting types, messages, and exception behavior — which prevents regressions when factory logic changes. Third, you will practice deciding between mocking and stubbing; stubs return simple canned data while mocks let you assert how a collaborator was used. That distinction keeps tests readable and reliable. Fourth, you will learn to spot common mistakes: over-mocking that creates brittle tests, or using real external services that turn unit tests into slow integration tests. These skills make tests faster, easier to maintain, and more focused on the behavior your team relies on during refactors.

The Strategy pattern separates an algorithm behind a common interface so different implementations can be swapped at runtime. For testing, that separation is useful: you test each concrete strategy in isolation to confirm its algorithmic behavior, and you test the context to ensure it delegates to the injected strategy. A practical example is a payment system: concrete strategies implement IPaymentStrategy and a PaymentContext invokes ProcessPayment. In a unit test for PaymentContext, we replace the concrete strategy with a mock and verify that ProcessPayment was called with the right amount. This avoids invoking real payment flows and keeps the test fast and deterministic. For each concrete strategy, write focused tests that exercise the algorithm it implements — for example, a credit card strategy may format fees differently than a PayPal strategy. A common misconception is to test that the Strategy pattern itself functions rather than asserting your code's delegation and result handling; tests should prove that PaymentContext uses the strategy contract properly and that strategies produce correct outputs. Example assertions include verifying call counts and parameters and ensuring alternate strategies are honored after SetStrategy is called. As a takeaway, treat strategies as units to test directly and treat the context as the orchestration point whose job is delegation and handling the returned result or side effects.

Factory patterns centralize object creation, so tests must verify both the factory's decision logic and the created objects' behavior. When testing a factory, create tests that exercise different input parameters and assert the returned concrete type and its observable behavior. For example, a VehicleFactory that returns Car or Motorcycle should be tested with CreateVehicle("Car") and CreateVehicle("Motorcycle"), asserting type and behavior like GetDescription. You should also test failure paths like unknown inputs to ensure the factory throws appropriate exceptions. A common misconception is to test only the produced type and not the object's behavior; always follow up type assertions with behavior checks on the returned object to ensure it meets expectations. If a factory depends on collaborators, mock those dependencies and verify they are used correctly during creation. When the factory logic is simple, the tests are straightforward: assert type and output. If creation is more complex, include tests that examine the factory's interactions with its dependencies. Balancing these tests prevents regression in object composition and ensures the system receives correctly configured instances during runtime. Testing the Factory Pattern means factories should be tested for the correct concrete type, expected behavior on the returned object, and proper exception handling.. In practical terms, assert created types, return behavior, and error cases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Decorator wraps a component to add responsibilities while preserving the wrapped component's interface. Testing a decorator requires asserting two things: first, that the decorator performs its additional behavior; second, that it delegates to the wrapped component so original behavior remains. For instance, a LoggingNotifierDecorator logs messages before and after calling the wrapped INotifier. In tests, replace the wrapped notifier and logger with mocks. Verify that the logger's LogInfo is called before and after, and that the wrapped notifier's Send is called exactly once with the expected message. A common mistake is to use the real wrapped component and real logger, which hides whether delegation and logging sequence are correct and complicates assertions. Use mocking to verify ordering and counts when the sequence matters. Another practical point: prefer verifying observable side effects or interaction counts rather than internal state. For critical paths, complement interaction tests with a light integration test using a ConsoleLogger or a fake logger to ensure the combined behavior looks correct in a more realistic run. This balanced approach keeps tests fast and trustworthy while guarding important sequences.

Mocking and stubbing are core techniques to isolate the unit under test. A stub provides canned responses and is useful when a collaborator returns predictable data you depend on. A mock, by contrast, is used when you want to verify how a dependency was used — the methods called, the arguments passed, and how often those calls occurred. In. NET, libraries like Moq make this straightforward: create Mock<T> objects, set up return values for stubs, and call Verify to assert interactions. Start each test by asking: do I care about the collaborator's behavior or only the interaction? If you only need a value, a stub suffices. If you need to assert a call sequence or argument values, use a mock with Verify. Avoid the anti-pattern of mocking everything; over-mocking can make tests brittle because internal changes in collaborators will break tests that shouldn't depend on those details. Instead, mock boundaries where your unit integrates with side effects, and keep simple data providers as lightweight fakes or stubs. When external services or databases are involved, use integration tests or well-controlled test doubles that mimic essential behavior without adding fragility. This decision process will keep tests fast, meaningful, and maintainable.

Unit tests and integration tests serve different goals and both matter in pattern-rich codebases. Unit tests isolate a small unit — typically a class — and verify its behavior in controlled conditions. They are fast, deterministic, and ideal for verifying delegation, algorithmic logic, and interaction with mocked collaborators. Integration tests, by contrast, verify how multiple components work together, possibly including database contexts, serialization, or external services (faked or real). For patterns like Factory, Strategy, and Decorator, unit tests confirm the internals and interactions, while a small set of integration tests can validate that constructed objects function correctly in realistic flows. A common error is relying only on integration tests; they can be slower and make it harder to find the exact failure point. Another mistake is using unit tests for scenarios that require end-to-end behavior, for example when database or configuration interactions are part of the correctness criteria. The recommended workflow is a large suite of focused unit tests for fast feedback, plus a smaller number of integration tests for confidence in critical paths. This mix keeps your feedback cycle short while ensuring the system behaves correctly when components are composed.

One widespread pitfall is over-mocking: mocking every dependency, including simple data providers, which makes tests brittle because they depend on internal implementation details. Another mistake is testing the pattern rather than the implementation — for example, writing tests that assert "this is a Strategy" instead of verifying that PaymentContext calls ProcessPayment with the correct amount. Also, developers sometimes blur the line between unit and integration tests by allowing real services or databases into unit tests; that reduces speed and makes failures harder to diagnose. To avoid these problems, mock only those collaborators that produce side effects or whose behavior you must verify. Use stubs or simple fakes for data providers, and keep integration tests separate and limited in number. Finally, keep your assertions focused on observable behavior and public contracts. Tests that assert interactions, return values, and exception behavior provide clear documentation and safe refactor points without coupling to internal implementation details.
